title: Intelligent human-centric lighting for mental wellbeing improvement
research_question: How can an intelligent human-centric lighting system, which adjusts light color based on detected human emotions and time of day, positively influence people's mental wellbeing?

participants.description: Ten participants tested the system in a real-world office environment. No further demographics provided.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: An intelligent lighting system consisting of LED strips installed in a real-world office environment. The system dynamically adjusts light color based on detected human emotions (angry, sad, happy, neutral) and time of day (day/night), following principles of color psychology.

findings.antecedent: Intelligent lighting system's pace of color changes (every 1 minute)
findings.mechanism: Mood is not likely to change that fast, suggesting slower transitions are preferred.

mechanisms: Color psychology: Light waves processed in the hypothalamus influence emotions and mood.
Circadian rhythms: Blue light at night can disrupt hormone flow; dynamic lighting can support natural rhythms.
Mood modulation: Specific colors and light can affect emotions, mood, and cognition.
Visual acuity: Adding more blue to light can increase clarity of vision.
Perception: Factors like light amount and spectral distributions influence perception of day course and energy levels.
Productivity: High correlated color temperature fluorescent lights can enhance wellbeing and productivity.
Autonomous system operation reduces distractions from manual configuration.
Mood changes are not rapid, so frequent light adjustments are unnecessary and potentially distracting.
Abrupt transitions between colors can be distracting or less pleasing.
implementation_implications: Implement gradual fading transitions between colors over a longer timeframe (e.g., 5 minutes) to be more subtle and less distracting.
Extend the time frame between consecutive emotion detections and light adjustments to more than one minute, as mood changes are not rapid.
Store and analyze user inputs from a mobile application to personalize lighting preferences and enhance system performance.
Develop a more robust emotional detection model to achieve higher accuracy.
Incorporate wearable devices (e.g., heart rate, physical movements) to acquire additional physiological information for more accurate emotional state assessment.
Conduct further research on extracting individual states and emotions from vital signals and integrating them into the system architecture.
Consider emotion and mood in groups of people, analyzing multiple users' emotions to set a weighted average color output.
Execute more scenarios and user test cases in diverse environments (in-home health care, smart home, industrial) to better understand system impact and gather preferences.
Replace custom hardware parts with existing commercial solutions for improved visual and performance results.
Integrate the HCL system into cognitive healthcare platforms like CHECkuP to influence patients' health and wellbeing.

tables.description: Mapping of color responses according to emotion and daytime.
Results of questionnaires, showing mean scores (1-5 scale) for color correctness, pace of changes, impact on mood, disturbance, and overall wellbeing from 10 participants.

limitations: The emotion detection model achieved an accuracy of 66%, which is considered sufficient for a prototype but requires improvement for more accurate results.
Participants reported that the transition between colors was too sharp and distracting, suggesting a need for more subtle changes.
The 1-minute time frame between consecutive light adjustments was perceived as too frequent, as mood does not change that rapidly.
Observations in real conditions showed that sad or neutral emotions were detected most of the time, and people often do not show emotions for prolonged periods.
The evaluation of participants' wellbeing was based on subjective statements, which might have been influenced by their enthusiasm for seeing the system in action (potential bias).
The study involved a small sample size (10 participants), limiting generalizability.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Intelligent human-centric lighting for mental wellbeing improvement
paper_metadata.crossref_journal: International Journal of Distributed Sensor Networks
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: In recent years, the main area of interest in the issue of influencing mental states of people is the impact of lighting on human beings, their wellbeing but also workplace productivity. This work discusses in detail the problem of positively influencing people using intelligent technologies, especially the role of the colors. We describe techniques and technologies needed to implement the case study of an intelligent lighting system. The system proposed can detect humans from an IP camera, find faces, and detect emotion. The main aim is to adjust the lights accordingly to the emotional result to improve the mood of people while taking into consideration the principles of color psychology and daytime. We have evaluated our case study solution in a real-world environment and collected the feedback from participants in the form of a questionnaire. Evaluation of participants’ wellbeing was based on their subjective statements. There were several ideas on further functionality extension which needs to be explored. Among them is including wearable devices to the proposed system, validate the emotional results according to them, but also determine the impact of an increasing number of users interacting with the system at the same time.
